title: A Bohmian version of a 2-state quantum system
abstract: I construct a Bohmian version of a 2-state quantum system, where in addition to the quantum state, the system is characterized by a definite physical state which changes stochastically under the guidance of the quantum state. I argue that the probabilities produced by this process are well-defined, contrary to claims in "Why quantum mechanics cannot be formulated as a Markov process" by D. Gillespie (1994) about a related model.
summary: The paper develops a Bohmian mechanical description for a simple two-state quantum system where the physical state undergoes stochastic jumps guided by the quantum wave function. The authors rigorously prove that this model is mathematically consistent, successfully refuting prior claims that such a formulation must fail due to issues related to Markov process assumptions.
main_problem: To construct a mathematically consistent Bohmian interpretation for a two-state quantum system, specifically addressing criticisms from related models regarding the validity of stochastic jump rates.
main_result: The authors demonstrate that the proposed Bohmian dynamics for the 2-state system are internally consistent, showing that the derived probability flow and conditional probabilities do not contradict established quantum mechanical expectations or critiques based on Markov process assumptions.

main_assumptions: The derivation assumes differentiability of conditional probabilities with respect to time, and it focuses on the two-state case, which does not guarantee general validity for all quantum systems.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the basic Bohmian dynamics using rate equations derived from the Schrödinger equation. It then rigorously derives these rates by analyzing conditional probabilities over small time intervals, culminating in a direct rebuttal of prior theoretical criticisms regarding process consistency.
why_interesting: This work tackles foundational issues at the intersection of quantum foundations and open systems theory, providing a detailed mathematical framework for interpreting stochastic jumps within a non-Markovian (or modified Markovian) context.
